1.1: From fairest creatures we desire increase,
1.2: That thereby beauty’s rose might never die,
1.3: But as the riper should by time decease,
1.4: His tender heir might bear his memory:
1.5: But thou, contracted to thine own bright eyes,
1.6: Feed’st thy light’s flame with self-substantial fuel,
1.7: Making a famine where abundance lies,
1.8: Thyself thy foe, to thy sweet self too cruel.
1.9: Thou that art now the world’s fresh ornament
1.10: And only herald to the gaudy spring,
1.11: Within thine own bud buriest thy content
1.12: And, tender churl, makest waste in niggarding.
1.13: Pity the world, or else this glutton be,
1.14: To eat the world’s due, by the grave and thee.
2.1: When forty winters shall besiege thy brow,
2.2: And dig deep trenches in thy beauty’s field,
2.3: Thy youth’s proud livery so gazed on now,
2.4: Will be a tatter’d weed, of small worth held:
2.5: Then being asked where all thy beauty lies,
2.6: Where all the treasure of thy lusty days,
2.7: To say, within thine own deep-sunken eyes,
2.8: Were an all-eating shame and thriftless praise.
2.9: How much more praise deserved thy beauty’s use,
2.10: If thou couldst answer “This fair child of mine
2.11: Shall sum my count and make my old excuse,”
2.12: Proving his beauty by succession thine!
2.13: This were to be new made when thou art old,
2.14: And see thy blood warm when thou feel’st it cold.
3.1: Look in thy glass, and tell the face thou viewest
3.2: Now is the time that face should form another;
3.3: Whose fresh repair if now thou not renewest,
3.4: Thou dost beguile the world, unbless some mother.
3.5: For where is she so fair whose unear’d womb
3.6: Disdains the tillage of thy husbandry?
3.7: Or who is he so fond will be the tomb
3.8: Of his self-love, to stop posterity?
3.9: Thou art thy mother’s glass, and she in thee
3.10: Calls back the lovely April of her prime:
3.11: So thou through windows of thine age shalt see
3.12: Despite of wrinkles this thy golden time.
3.13: But if thou live, remember’d not to be,
3.14: Die single, and thine image dies with thee.
4.1: Unthrifty loveliness, why dost thou spend
4.3: Nature’s bequest gives nothing but doth lend,
4.4: And being frank she lends to those are free.
4.5: Then, beauteous niggard, why dost thou abuse
4.6: The bounteous largess given thee to give?
4.7: Profitless usurer, why dost thou use
4.8: So great a sum of sums, yet canst not live?
4.9: For having traffic with thyself alone,
4.10: Thou of thyself thy sweet self dost deceive.
4.11: Then how, when nature calls thee to be gone,
4.12: What acceptable audit canst thou leave?
4.13: Thy unused beauty must be tomb’d with thee,
4.14: Which, used, lives th’ executor to be.
5.1: Those hours, that with gentle work did frame
5.2: The lovely gaze where every eye doth dwell,
5.3: Will play the tyrants to the very same
5.4: And that unfair which fairly doth excel;
5.5: For never-resting time leads summer on
5.6: To hideous winter and confounds him there;
5.7: Sap check’d with frost and lusty leaves quite gone,
5.8: Beauty o’ersnowed and bareness every where:
5.9: Then, were not summer’s distillation left,
5.10: A liquid prisoner pent in walls of glass,
5.11: Beauty’s effect with beauty were bereft,
5.12: Nor it nor no remembrance what it was:
5.13: But flowers distill’d, though they with winter meet,
5.14: Leese but their show; their substance still lives sweet.
6.1: Then let not winter’s ragged hand deface
6.2: In thee thy summer, ere thou be distill’d:
6.3: Make sweet some vial; treasure thou some place
6.4: With beauty’s treasure, ere it be self-kill’d.
6.5: That use is not forbidden usury
6.6: Which happies those that pay the willing loan;
6.7: That’s for thyself to breed another thee,
6.8: Or ten times happier, be it ten for one;
6.9: Ten times thyself were happier than thou art,
6.10: If ten of thine ten times refigured thee:
6.11: Then what could death do, if thou shouldst depart,
6.13: Be not self-will’d, for thou art much too fair
6.14: To be death’s conquest and make worms thine heir.
7.1: Lo! in the orient when the gracious light
7.2: Lifts up his burning head, each under eye
7.3: Doth homage to his new-appearing sight,
7.4: Serving with looks his sacred majesty;
7.5: And having climb’d the steep-up heavenly hill,
7.6: Resembling strong youth in his middle age,
7.7: Yet mortal looks adore his beauty still,
7.9: But when from highmost pitch, with weary car,
7.10: Like feeble age, he reeleth from the day,
7.11: The eyes, ’fore duteous, now converted are
7.12: From his low tract and look another way:
7.13: So thou, thyself out-going in thy noon,
7.14: Unlook’d on diest, unless thou get a son.
8.1: Music to hear, why hear’st thou music sadly?
8.2: Sweets with sweets war not, joy delights in joy.
8.3: Why lovest thou that which thou receivest not gladly,
8.4: Or else receivest with pleasure thine annoy?
8.5: If the true concord of well-tuned sounds,
8.6: By unions married, do offend thine ear,
8.7: They do but sweetly chide thee, who confounds
8.8: In singleness the parts that thou shouldst bear.
8.9: Mark how one string, sweet husband to another,
8.10: Strikes each in each by mutual ordering,
8.11: Resembling sire and child and happy mother
8.12: Who all in one, one pleasing note do sing:
8.13: Whose speechless song, being many, seeming one,
8.14: Sings this to thee: “Thou single wilt prove none.”
9.1: Is it for fear to wet a widow’s eye
9.2: That thou consumest thyself in single life?
9.3: Ah! if thou issueless shalt hap to die,
9.4: The world will wail thee, like a makeless wife;
9.5: The world will be thy widow and still weep
9.6: That thou no form of thee hast left behind,
9.7: When every private widow well may keep
9.8: By children’s eyes her husband’s shape in mind.
9.9: Look, what an unthrift in the world doth spend
9.10: Shifts but his place, for still the world enjoys it;
9.11: But beauty’s waste hath in the world an end,
9.12: And kept unused, the user so destroys it.
9.13: No love toward others in that bosom sits
9.14: That on himself such murderous shame commits.
10.1: For shame! deny that thou bear’st love to any,
10.2: Who for thyself art so unprovident.
10.3: Grant, if thou wilt, thou art beloved of many,
10.4: But that thou none lovest is most evident;
10.5: For thou art so possess’d with murderous hate
10.6: That ’gainst thyself thou stick’st not to conspire,
10.7: Seeking that beauteous roof to ruinate
10.8: Which to repair should be thy chief desire.
10.9: O, change thy thought, that I may change my mind!
10.10: Shall hate be fairer lodged than gentle love?
10.11: Be, as thy presence is, gracious and kind,
10.12: Or to thyself at least kind-hearted prove:
10.13: Make thee another self, for love of me,
10.14: That beauty still may live in thine or thee.
11.1: As fast as thou shalt wane, so fast thou growest
11.2: In one of thine, from that which thou departest;
11.3: And that fresh blood which youngly thou bestowest
11.4: Thou mayst call thine when thou from youth convertest.
11.5: Herein lives wisdom, beauty and increase;
11.6: Without this, folly, age and cold decay:
11.7: If all were minded so, the times should cease
11.8: And threescore year would make the world away.
11.9: Let those whom Nature hath not made for store,
11.10: Harsh featureless and rude, barrenly perish:
11.11: Look, whom she best endow’d she gave the more;
11.12: Which bounteous gift thou shouldst in bounty cherish:
11.13: She carved thee for her seal, and meant thereby
11.14: Thou shouldst print more, not let that copy die.
12.1: When I do count the clock that tells the time,
12.2: And see the brave day sunk in hideous night;
12.3: When I behold the violet past prime,
12.4: And sable curls all silver’d o’er with white;
12.5: When lofty trees I see barren of leaves
12.6: Which erst from heat did canopy the herd,
12.7: And summer’s green all girded up in sheaves
12.8: Borne on the bier with white and bristly beard,
12.9: Then of thy beauty do I question make,
12.10: That thou among the wastes of time must go,
12.11: Since sweets and beauties do themselves forsake
12.12: And die as fast as they see others grow;
12.13: And nothing ’gainst Time’s scythe can make defence
12.14: Save breed, to brave him when he takes thee hence.
13.1: O, that you were yourself! but, love, you are
13.2: No longer yours than you yourself here live:
13.3: Against this coming end you should prepare,
13.4: And your sweet semblance to some other give.
13.5: So should that beauty which you hold in lease
13.6: Find no determination; then you were
13.8: When your sweet issue your sweet form should bear.
13.9: Who lets so fair a house fall to decay,
13.10: Which husbandry in honour might uphold
13.11: Against the stormy gusts of winter’s day
13.12: And barren rage of death’s eternal cold?
13.13: O, none but unthrifts! Dear my love, you know
13.14: You had a father: let your son say so.
14.1: Not from the stars do I my judgement pluck;
14.2: And yet methinks I have astronomy,
14.3: But not to tell of good or evil luck,
14.4: Of plagues, of dearths, or seasons’ quality;
14.5: Nor can I fortune to brief minutes tell,
14.6: Pointing to each his thunder, rain and wind,
14.7: Or say with princes if it shall go well,
14.8: By oft predict that I in heaven find:
14.9: But from thine eyes my knowledge I derive,
14.10: And, constant stars, in them I read such art
14.11: As truth and beauty shall together thrive,
14.12: If from thyself to store thou wouldst convert;
14.13: Or else of thee this I prognosticate:
14.14: Thy end is truth’s and beauty’s doom and date.
15.1: When I consider everything that grows
15.2: Holds in perfection but a little moment,
15.3: That this huge stage presenteth nought but shows
15.4: Whereon the stars in secret influence comment;
15.5: When I perceive that men as plants increase,
15.6: Cheered and check’d even by the self-same sky,
15.7: Vaunt in their youthful sap, at height decrease,
15.8: And wear their brave state out of memory;
15.9: Then the conceit of this inconstant stay
15.10: Sets you most rich in youth before my sight,
15.11: Where wasteful Time debateth with Decay,
15.12: To change your day of youth to sullied night;
15.13: And all in war with Time for love of you,
15.14: As he takes from you, I engraft you new.
16.1: But wherefore do not you a mightier way
16.2: Make war upon this bloody tyrant, Time?
16.3: And fortify yourself in your decay
16.4: With means more blessed than my barren rhyme?
16.5: Now stand you on the top of happy hours,
16.6: And many maiden gardens yet unset
16.7: With virtuous wish would bear you living flowers,
16.8: Much liker than your painted counterfeit:
16.9: So should the lines of life that life repair,
16.10: Which this, Time’s pencil, or my pupil pen,
16.11: Neither in inward worth nor outward fair,
16.12: Can make you live yourself in eyes of men.
16.13: To give away yourself keeps yourself still,
16.14: And you must live, drawn by your own sweet skill.
17.1: Who will believe my verse in time to come,
17.2: If it were fill’d with your most high deserts?
17.3: Though yet, heaven knows, it is but as a tomb
17.4: Which hides your life and shows not half your parts.
17.5: If I could write the beauty of your eyes
17.6: And in fresh numbers number all your graces,
17.7: The age to come would say “this poet lies;
17.8: Such heavenly touches ne’er touch’d earthly faces.”
17.9: So should my papers yellow’d with their age
17.10: Be scorn’d like old men of less truth than tongue,
17.11: And your true rights be term’d a poet’s rage
17.12: And stretched metre of an antique song:
17.13: But were some child of yours alive that time,
17.14: You should live twice; in it and in my rhyme.
18.1: Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
18.2: Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
18.3: Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
18.4: And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
18.5: Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
18.6: And often is his gold complexion dimm’d;
18.7: And every fair from fair sometime declines,
18.8: By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d;
18.9: But thy eternal summer shall not fade
18.10: Nor lose possession of that fair thou owest;
18.11: Nor shall Death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
18.12: When in eternal lines to time thou growest:
18.13: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
18.14: So long lives this and this gives life to thee.
19.1: Devouring Time, blunt thou the lion’s paws,
19.2: And make the earth devour her own sweet brood;
19.3: Pluck the keen teeth from the fierce tiger’s jaws,
19.4: And burn the long-lived phoenix in her blood;
19.5: Make glad and sorry seasons as thou fleets,
19.6: And do whate’er thou wilt, swift-footed Time,
19.7: To the wide world and all her fading sweets;
19.8: But I forbid thee one most heinous crime:
19.9: O, carve not with thy hours my love’s fair brow,
19.10: Nor draw no lines there with thine antique pen;
19.11: Him in thy course untainted do allow
19.12: For beauty’s pattern to succeeding men.
19.13: Yet, do thy worst, old Time: despite thy wrong,
19.14: My love shall in my verse ever live young.
20.1: A woman’s face with Nature’s own hand painted
20.2: Hast thou, the master-mistress of my passion;
20.3: A woman’s gentle heart, but not acquainted
20.4: With shifting change, as is false women’s fashion;
20.5: An eye more bright than theirs, less false in rolling,
20.6: Gilding the object whereupon it gazeth;
20.7: A man in hue, all “hues” in his controlling,
20.8: Which steals men’s eyes and women’s souls amazeth.
20.9: And for a woman wert thou first created;
20.10: Till Nature, as she wrought thee, fell a-doting,
20.11: And by addition me of thee defeated,
20.12: By adding one thing to my purpose nothing.
20.13: But since she prick’d thee out for women’s pleasure,
20.14: Mine be thy love and thy love’s use their treasure.
21.1: So is it not with me as with that Muse
21.2: Stirr’d by a painted beauty to his verse,
21.3: Who heaven itself for ornament doth use
21.4: And every fair with his fair doth rehearse;
21.5: Making a couplement of proud compare,
21.6: With sun and moon, with earth and sea’s rich gems,
21.7: With April’s first-born flowers, and all things rare
21.8: That heaven’s air in this huge rondure hems.
21.9: O, let me, true in love, but truly write,
21.10: And then believe me, my love is as fair
21.11: As any mother’s child, though not so bright
21.12: As those gold candles fix’d in heaven’s air:
21.13: Let them say more that like of hearsay well;
21.14: I will not praise that purpose not to sell.
22.1: My glass shall not persuade me I am old,
22.2: So long as youth and thou are of one date;
22.3: But when in thee time’s furrows I behold,
22.4: Then look I death my days should expiate.
22.5: For all that beauty that doth cover thee
22.6: Is but the seemly raiment of my heart,
22.7: Which in thy breast doth live, as thine in me:
22.8: How can I then be elder than thou art?
22.9: O, therefore, love, be of thyself so wary
22.10: As I not for myself, but for thee will;
22.11: Bearing thy heart which I will keep so chary
22.12: As tender nurse her babe from faring ill.
22.13: Presume not on thy heart when mine is slain;
22.14: Thou gavest me thine, not to give back again.
23.1: As an unperfect actor on the stage
23.2: Who with his fear is put beside his part,
23.3: Or some fierce thing replete with too much rage,
23.4: Whose strength’s abundance weakens his own heart,
23.5: So I, for fear of trust, forget to say
23.6: The perfect ceremony of love’s rite,
23.7: And in mine own love’s strength seem to decay,
23.8: O’ercharged with burden of mine own love’s might.
23.9: O, let my looks be then the eloquence
23.10: And dumb presagers of my speaking breast,
23.11: Who plead for love and look for recompense
23.12: More than that tongue that more hath more express’d.
23.13: O, learn to read what silent love hath writ:
23.14: To hear with eyes belongs to love’s fine wit.
24.1: Mine eye hath play’d the painter and hath stell’d
24.2: Thy beauty’s form in table of my heart;
24.3: My body is the frame wherein ’tis held,
24.4: And perspective it is best painter’s art.
24.5: For through the painter must you see his skill,
24.6: To find where your true image pictured lies;
24.7: Which in my bosom’s shop is hanging still,
24.8: That hath his windows glazed with thine eyes.
24.9: Now see what good turns eyes for eyes have done:
24.10: Mine eyes have drawn thy shape, and thine for me
24.11: Are windows to my breast, where-through the sun
24.12: Delights to peep, to gaze therein on thee;
24.13: Yet eyes this cunning want to grace their art;
24.14: They draw but what they see, know not the heart.
25.1: Let those who are in favour with their stars
25.2: Of public honour and proud titles boast,
25.3: Whilst I, whom fortune of such triumph bars,
25.4: Unlook’d for joy in that I honour most.
25.5: Great princes’ favourites their fair leaves spread
25.6: But as the marigold at the sun’s eye,
25.7: And in themselves their pride lies buried,
25.8: For at a frown they in their glory die.
25.9: The painful warrior famoused for fight,
25.10: After a thousand victories once foil’d,
25.11: Is from the book of honour razed quite,
25.12: And all the rest forgot for which he toil’d:
25.13: Then happy I, that love and am beloved
25.14: Where I may not remove nor be removed.
26.1: Lord of my love, to whom in vassalage
26.2: Thy merit hath my duty strongly knit,
26.3: To thee I send this written embassage,
26.4: To witness duty, not to show my wit:
26.5: Duty so great, which wit so poor as mine
26.6: May make seem bare, in wanting words to show it,
26.7: But that I hope some good conceit of thine
26.8: In thy soul’s thought, all naked, will bestow it;
26.9: Till whatsoever star that guides my moving
26.10: Points on me graciously with fair aspect
26.11: And puts apparel on my tatter’d loving,
26.12: To show me worthy of thy sweet respect:
26.13: Then may I dare to boast how I do love thee;
26.14: Till then not show my head where thou mayst prove me.
27.1: Weary with toil, I haste me to my bed,
27.2: The dear respose for limbs with travel tired;
27.3: But then begins a journey in my head,
27.4: To work my mind, when body’s work’s expired:
27.5: For then my thoughts, from far where I abide,
27.6: Intend a zealous pilgrimage to thee,
27.7: And keep my drooping eyelids open wide,
27.8: Looking on darkness which the blind do see:
27.9: Save that my soul’s imaginary sight
27.10: Presents thy shadow to my sightless view,
27.11: Which, like a jewel hung in ghastly night,
27.12: Makes black night beauteous and her old face new.
27.13: Lo! thus, by day my limbs, by night my mind,
27.14: For thee and for myself no quiet find.
28.1: How can I then return in happy plight,
28.2: That am debarr’d the benefit of rest?
28.3: When day’s oppression is not eased by night,
28.4: But day by night, and night by day, oppress’d?
28.5: And each, though enemies to either’s reign,
28.6: Do in consent shake hands to torture me;
28.7: The one by toil, the other to complain
28.8: How far I toil, still farther off from thee.
28.9: I tell the day, to please him thou art bright
28.10: And dost him grace when clouds do blot the heaven:
28.11: So flatter I the swart-complexion’d night,
28.12: When sparkling stars twire not thou gild’st the even.
28.13: But day doth daily draw my sorrows longer
28.14: And night doth nightly make grief’s length seem stronger.
29.1: When, in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes,
29.2: I all alone beweep my outcast state
29.3: And trouble deaf heaven with my bootless cries
29.4: And look upon myself and curse my fate,
29.5: Wishing me like to one more rich in hope,
29.6: Featured like him, like him with friends possess’d,
29.7: Desiring this man’s art and that man’s scope,
29.8: With what I most enjoy contented least;
29.9: Yet in these thoughts myself almost despising,
29.10: Haply I think on thee, and then my state,
29.11: Like to the lark at break of day arising
29.12: From sullen earth, sings hymns at heaven’s gate;
29.13: For thy sweet love remember’d such wealth brings
29.14: That then I scorn to change my state with kings.
30.1: When to the sessions of sweet silent thought
30.2: I summon up remembrance of things past,
30.3: I sigh the lack of many a thing I sought,
30.4: And with old woes new wail my dear time’s waste:
30.5: Then can I drown an eye, unused to flow,
30.6: For precious friends hid in death’s dateless night,
30.7: And weep afresh love’s long since cancell’d woe,
30.8: And moan the expense of many a vanish’d sight:
30.9: Then can I grieve at grievances foregone,
30.10: And heavily from woe to woe tell o’er
30.11: The sad account of fore-bemoaned moan,
30.12: Which I new pay as if not paid before.
30.13: But if the while I think on thee, dear friend,
30.14: All losses are restored and sorrows end.
31.1: Thy bosom is endeared with all hearts,
31.2: Which I by lacking have supposed dead,
31.3: And there reigns love and all love’s loving parts,
31.4: And all those friends which I thought buried.
31.5: How many a holy and obsequious tear
31.6: Hath dear religious love stol’n from mine eye
31.7: As interest of the dead, which now appear
31.8: But things removed that hidden in thee lie!
31.9: Thou art the grave where buried love doth live,
31.10: Hung with the trophies of my lovers gone,
31.11: Who all their parts of me to thee did give;
31.12: That due of many now is thine alone:
31.13: Their images I loved I view in thee,
31.14: And thou, all they, hast all the all of me.
32.1: If thou survive my well-contented day,
32.2: When that churl Death my bones with dust shall cover,
32.3: And shalt by fortune once more re-survey
32.4: These poor rude lines of thy deceased lover,
32.5: Compare them with the bettering of the time,
32.6: And though they be outstripp’d by every pen,
32.7: Reserve them for my love, not for their rhyme,
32.8: Exceeded by the height of happier men.
32.9: O, then vouchsafe me but this loving thought:
32.10: “Had my friend’s Muse grown with this growing age,
32.11: A dearer birth than this his love had brought,
32.12: To march in ranks of better equipage:
32.13: But since he died and poets better prove,
32.14: Theirs for their style I’ll read, his for his love.”
33.1: Full many a glorious morning have I seen
33.2: Flatter the mountain tops with sovereign eye,
33.3: Kissing with golden face the meadows green,
33.4: Gilding pale streams with heavenly alchemy;
33.5: Anon permit the basest clouds to ride
33.6: With ugly rack on his celestial face,
33.7: And from the forlorn world his visage hide,
33.8: Stealing unseen to west with this disgrace:
33.9: Even so my sun one early morn did shine
33.10: With all-triumphant splendour on my brow;
33.11: But out, alack! he was but one hour mine;
33.12: The region cloud hath mask’d him from me now.
33.13: Yet him for this my love no whit disdaineth;
33.14: Suns of the world may stain when heaven’s sun staineth.
34.1: Why didst thou promise such a beauteous day
34.2: And make me travel forth without my cloak,
34.3: To let base clouds o’ertake me in my way,
34.4: Hiding thy bravery in their rotten smoke?
34.5: ’Tis not enough that through the cloud thou break,
34.6: To dry the rain on my storm-beaten face,
34.7: For no man well of such a salve can speak
34.8: That heals the wound and cures not the disgrace:
34.9: Nor can thy shame give physic to my grief;
34.10: Though thou repent, yet I have still the loss:
34.11: The offender’s sorrow lends but weak relief
34.12: To him that bears the strong offence’s cross.
34.13: Ah! but those tears are pearl which thy love sheds,
34.14: And they are rich and ransom all ill deeds.
35.1: No more be grieved at that which thou hast done:
35.2: Roses have thorns, and silver fountains mud;
35.3: Clouds and eclipses stain both moon and sun,
35.4: And loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud.
35.5: All men make faults, and even I in this,
35.8: Excusing thy sins more than thy sins are;
35.9: For to thy sensual fault I bring in sense⁠—
35.10: Thy adverse party is thy advocate⁠—
35.11: And ’gainst myself a lawful plea commence:

36.1: Let me confess that we two must be twain,
36.2: Although our undivided loves are one:
36.3: So shall those blots that do with me remain
36.4: Without thy help by me be borne alone.
36.5: In our two loves there is but one respect,
36.6: Though in our lives a separable spite,
36.7: Which though it alter not love’s sole effect,
36.8: Yet doth it steal sweet hours from love’s delight.
36.9: I may not evermore acknowledge thee,
36.10: Lest my bewailed guilt should do thee shame,
36.11: Nor thou with public kindness honour me,
36.12: Unless thou take that honour from thy name:

36.14: As, thou being mine, mine is thy good report.
37.1: As a decrepit father takes delight
37.2: To see his active child do deeds of youth,
37.3: So I, made lame by fortune’s dearest spite,
37.4: Take all my comfort of thy worth and truth.
37.5: For whether beauty, birth, or wealth, or wit,
37.6: Or any of these all, or all, or more,
37.7: Entitled in thy parts do crowned sit,
37.8: I make my love engrafted to this store:
37.9: So then I am not lame, poor, nor despised,
37.10: Whilst that this shadow doth such substance give
37.11: That I in thy abundance am sufficed
37.12: And by a part of all thy glory live.
37.13: Look, what is best, that best I wish in thee:
37.14: This wish I have; then ten times happy me!
38.1: How can my Muse want subject to invent,
38.2: While thou dost breathe, that pour’st into my verse
38.3: Thine own sweet argument, too excellent
38.4: For every vulgar paper to rehearse?
38.5: O, give thyself the thanks, if aught in me
38.6: Worthy perusal stand against thy sight;

38.8: When thou thyself dost give invention light?
38.9: Be thou the tenth Muse, ten times more in worth
38.10: Than those old nine which rhymers invocate;
38.11: And he that calls on thee, let him bring forth
38.12: Eternal numbers to outlive long date.

38.14: The pain be mine, but thine shall be the praise.
39.1: O, how thy worth with manners may I sing,

39.3: What can mine own praise to mine own self bring?
39.4: And what is’t but mine own when I praise thee?

40.1: Take all my loves, my love, yea, take them all;

41.1: Those pretty wrongs that liberty commits,

42.3: That she hath thee, is of my wailing chief,
42.4: A loss in love that touches me more nearly.

43.1: When most I wink, then do mine eyes best see,
43.2: For all the day they view things unrespected;
43.3: But when I sleep, in dreams they look on thee,
43.4: And darkly bright are bright in dark directed.
43.5: Then thou, whose shadow shadows doth make bright,
43.6: How would thy shadow’s form form happy show
43.7: To the clear day with thy much clearer light,
43.8: When to unseeing eyes thy shade shines so!

43.10: By looking on thee in the living day,
43.11: When in dead night thy fair imperfect shade
43.12: Through heavy sleep on sightless eyes doth stay!

44.1: If the dull substance of my flesh were thought,
44.2: Injurious distance should not stop my way;
44.3: For then despite of space I would be brought,
44.4: From limits far remote, where thou dost stay.
44.5: No matter then although my foot did stand
44.6: Upon the farthest earth removed from thee;
44.7: For nimble thought can jump both sea and land
44.8: As soon as think the place where he would be.

44.10: To leap large lengths of miles when thou art gone,
44.11: But that so much of earth and water wrought
44.12: I must attend time’s leisure with my moan,
44.13: Receiving nought by elements so slow
44.14: But heavy tears, badges of either’s woe.
45.1: The other two, slight air and purging fire,
45.2: Are both with thee, wherever I abide;
45.3: The first my thought, the other my desire,
45.4: These present-absent with swift motion slide.

45.6: In tender embassy of love to thee,
45.7: My life, being made of four, with two alone
45.8: Sinks down to death, oppress’d with melancholy;
45.10: By those swift messengers return’d from thee,
45.11: Who even but now come back again, assured

46.1: Mine eye and heart are at a mortal war
46.2: How to divide the conquest of thy sight;
46.3: Mine eye my heart thy picture’s sight would bar,
46.4: My heart mine eye the freedom of that right.

46.7: But the defendant doth that plea deny

46.11: And by their verdict is determined
46.12: The clear eye’s moiety and the dear heart’s part:

47.1: Betwixt mine eye and heart a league is took,
47.2: And each doth good turns now unto the other:
47.3: When that mine eye is famish’d for a look,
47.4: Or heart in love with sighs himself doth smother,
47.5: With my love’s picture then my eye doth feast
47.6: And to the painted banquet bids my heart;
47.7: Another time mine eye is my heart’s guest
47.8: And in his thoughts of love doth share a part:
47.9: So, either by thy picture or my love,
47.10: Thyself away art present still with me;
47.11: For thou not farther than my thoughts canst move,
47.12: And I am still with them and they with thee;

47.14: Awakes my heart to heart’s and eye’s delight.
48.1: How careful was I, when I took my way,
48.2: Each trifle under truest bars to thrust,
48.3: That to my use it might unused stay
48.4: From hands of falsehood, in sure wards of trust!
48.5: But thou, to whom my jewels trifles are,
48.6: Most worthy comfort, now my greatest grief,
48.7: Thou, best of dearest and mine only care,
48.8: Art left the prey of every vulgar thief.
48.9: Thee have I not lock’d up in any chest,
48.10: Save where thou art not, though I feel thou art,
48.11: Within the gentle closure of my breast,
48.12: From whence at pleasure thou mayst come and part;

49.1: Against that time, if ever that time come,
49.2: When I shall see thee frown on my defects,
49.3: When as thy love hath cast his utmost sum,
49.4: Call’d to that audit by advised respects;
49.5: Against that time when thou shalt strangely pass
49.6: And scarcely greet me with that sun, thine eye,
49.7: When love, converted from the thing it was,
49.8: Shall reasons find of settled gravity⁠—
49.9: Against that time do I ensconce me here
49.10: Within the knowledge of mine own desert,
49.11: And this my hand against myself uprear,
49.12: To guard the lawful reasons on thy part:
49.13: To leave poor me thou hast the strength of laws,

50.1: How heavy do I journey on the way,
50.2: When what I seek, my weary travel’s end,
50.3: Doth teach that case and that repose to say
50.4: “Thus far the miles are measured from thy friend!”
50.5: The beast that bears me, tired with my woe,
50.6: Plods dully on, to bear that weight in me,
50.7: As if by some instinct the wretch did know
50.8: His rider loved not speed, being made from thee:
50.9: The bloody spur cannot provoke him on
50.10: That sometimes anger thrusts into his hide;
50.11: Which heavily he answers with a groan,
50.12: More sharp to me than spurring to his side;
50.13: For that same groan doth put this in my mind;
50.14: My grief lies onward and my joy behind.
51.1: Thus can my love excuse the slow offence
51.2: Of my dull bearer when from thee I speed:
51.3: From where thou art why should I haste me thence?
51.4: Till I return, of posting is no need.
51.5: O, what excuse will my poor beast then find,
51.6: When swift extremity can seem but slow?
51.7: Then should I spur, though mounted on the wind;
51.8: In winged speed no motion shall I know:
51.9: Then can no horse with my desire keep pace;
51.10: Therefore desire, of perfect’st love being made,
51.11: Shall neigh⁠—no dull flesh⁠—in his fiery race;
51.12: But love, for love, thus shall excuse my jade;
51.13: Since from thee going he went wilful-slow,
51.14: Towards thee I’ll run, and give him leave to go.
52.1: So am I as the rich, whose blessed key
52.2: Can bring him to his sweet up-locked treasure,
52.3: The which he will not every hour survey,
52.4: For blunting the fine point of seldom pleasure.
52.5: Therefore are feasts so solemn and so rare,
52.6: Since, seldom coming, in that long year set,
52.7: Like stones of worth they thinly placed are,
52.8: Or captain jewels in the carcanet.
52.9: So is the time that keeps you as my chest,
52.10: Or as the wardrobe which the robe doth hide,
52.11: To make some special instant special blest,
52.12: By new unfolding his imprison’d pride.
52.13: Blessed are you, whose worthiness gives scope,

54.1: O, how much more doth beauty beauteous seem
54.2: By that sweet ornament which truth doth give!
54.3: The rose looks fair, but fairer we it deem
54.4: For that sweet odour which doth in it live.
54.5: The canker-blooms have full as deep a dye
54.6: As the perfumed tincture of the roses,
54.7: Hang on such thorns and play as wantonly
54.8: When summer’s breath their masked buds discloses:
54.9: But, for their virtue only is their show,
54.10: They live unwoo’d and unrespected fade,
54.11: Die to themselves. Sweet roses do not so;
54.12: Of their sweet deaths are sweetest odours made:
54.13: And so of you, beauteous and lovely youth,
54.14: When that shall fade, my verse distills your truth.
55.1: Not marble, nor the gilded monuments
55.2: Of princes, shall outlive this powerful rhyme;
55.3: But you shall shine more bright in these contents
55.4: Than unswept stone besmear’d with sluttish time.
55.5: When wasteful war shall statues overturn,
55.6: And broils root out the work of masonry,
55.7: Nor Mars his sword nor war’s quick fire shall burn
55.8: The living record of your memory.
55.10: Shall you pace forth; your praise shall still find room
55.11: Even in the eyes of all posterity
55.12: That wear this world out to the ending doom.
55.13: So, till the judgment that yourself arise,
55.14: You live in this, and dwell in lovers’ eyes.
56.1: Sweet love, renew thy force; be it not said
56.2: Thy edge should blunter be than appetite,
56.3: Which but to-day by feeding is allay’d,
56.4: To-morrow sharpen’d in his former might:
56.5: So, love, be thou; although to-day thou fill
56.6: Thy hungry eyes even till they wink with fulness,
56.7: To-morrow see again, and do not kill
56.8: The spirit of love with a perpetual dullness.
56.9: Let this sad interim like the ocean be
56.10: Which parts the shore, where two contracted new
56.11: Come daily to the banks, that, when they see
56.12: Return of love, more blest may be the view;
56.13: Else call it winter, which being full of care
56.14: Makes summer’s welcome thrice more wish’d, more rare.
57.1: Being your slave, what should I do but tend
57.2: Upon the hours and times of your desire?
57.3: I have no precious time at all to spend,
57.4: Nor services to do, till you require.
57.5: Nor dare I chide the world-without-end hour
57.6: Whilst I, my sovereign, watch the clock for you,
57.7: Nor think the bitterness of absence sour
57.8: When you have bid your servant once adieu;
57.9: Nor dare I question with my jealous thought
57.10: Where you may be, or your affairs suppose,
57.11: But, like a sad slave, stay and think of nought
57.12: Save, where you are how happy you make those.
57.13: So true a fool is love that in your will,
57.14: Though you do anything, he thinks no ill.
58.1: That god forbid that made me first your slave,
58.2: I should in thought control your times of pleasure,
58.3: Or at your hand the account of hours to crave,
58.4: Being your vassal, bound to stay your leisure!

58.6: The imprison’d absence of your liberty;
58.7: And patience, tame to sufferance, bide each check,
58.9: Be where you list, your charter is so strong
58.10: That you yourself may privilage your time
58.11: To what you will; to you it doth belong

59.1: If there be nothing new, but that which is
59.2: Hath been before, how are our brains beguiled,
59.3: Which, labouring for invention, bear amiss
59.4: The second burthen of a former child!
59.5: O, that record could with a backward look,
59.6: Even of five hundred courses of the sun,
59.7: Show me your image in some antique book,
59.8: Since mind at first in character was done!
59.9: That I might see what the old world could say
59.10: To this composed wonder of your frame;

60.1: Like as the waves make towards the pebbled shore,
60.2: So do our minutes hasten to their end;
60.3: Each changing place with that which goes before,
60.4: In sequent toil all forwards do contend.
60.5: Nativity, once in the main of light,
60.6: Crawls to maturity, wherewith being crown’d,
60.8: And Time that gave doth now his gift confound.

60.10: And delves the parallels in beauty’s brow,
60.11: Feeds on the rarities of nature’s truth,

61.1: Is it thy will thy image should keep open
61.2: My heavy eyelids to the weary night?
61.3: Dost thou desire my slumbers should be broken,
61.4: While shadows like to thee do mock my sight?
61.5: Is it thy spirit that thou send’st from thee
61.6: So far from home into my deeds to pry,
61.7: To find out shames and idle hours in me,
61.8: The scope and tenour of thy jealousy?

61.11: Mine own true love that doth my rest defeat,

62.1: Sin of self-love possesseth all mine eye
62.2: And all my soul and all my every part;
62.3: And for this sin there is no remedy,
62.4: It is so grounded inward in my heart.
62.5: Methinks no face so gracious is as mine,
62.6: No shape so true, no truth of such account;

63.1: Against my love shall be, as I am now,

63.3: When hours have drain’d his blood and fill’d his brow
63.4: With lines and wrinkles; when his youthful morn
63.5: Hath travell’d on to age’s steepy night,

64.2: The rich proud cost of outworn buried age;

64.4: And brass eternal slave to mortal rage;

67.4: And lace itself with his society?

68.1: Thus is his cheek the map of days outworn,
68.2: When beauty lived and died as flowers do now,
68.3: Before these bastard signs of fair were born,
68.4: Or durst inhabit on a living brow;
68.5: Before the golden tresses of the dead,

69.2: Want nothing that the thought of hearts can mend;

70.1: That thou art blamed shall not be thy defect,

70.3: The ornament of beauty is suspect,
70.4: A crow that flies in heaven’s sweetest air.
