71.14: And mock you with me after I am gone.
72.1: O, lest the world should task you to recite
72.2: What merit lived in me, that you should love
72.3: After my death, dear love, forget me quite,
72.4: For you in me can nothing worthy prove;
72.5: Unless you would devise some virtuous lie,
72.6: To do more for me than mine own desert,
72.7: And hang more praise upon deceased I
72.8: Than niggard truth would willingly impart:
72.9: O, lest your true love may seem false in this,
72.10: That you for love speak well of me untrue,
72.11: My name be buried where my body is,
72.12: And live no more to shame nor me nor you.
72.13: For I am shamed by that which I bring forth,
72.14: And so should you, to love things nothing worth.
73.1: That time of year thou mayst in me behold
73.2: When yellow leaves, or none, or few, do hang
73.3: Upon those boughs which shake against the cold,
73.4: Bare ruin’d choirs, where late the sweet birds sang.
73.5: In me thou see’st the twilight of such day
73.6: As after sunset fadeth in the west,
73.7: Which by and by black night doth take away,
73.8: Death’s second self, that seals up all in rest.
73.9: In me thou see’st the glowing of such fire
73.10: That on the ashes of his youth doth lie,
73.11: As the death-bed whereon it must expire
73.12: Consumed with that which it was nourish’d by.
73.13: This thou perceivest, which makes thy love more strong,
73.14: To love that well which thou must leave ere long.
74.1: But be contented: when that fell arrest
74.2: Without all bail shall carry me away,
74.3: My life hath in this line some interest,
74.4: Which for memorial still with thee shall stay.
74.5: When thou reviewest this, thou dost review
74.6: The very part was consecrate to thee:
74.7: The earth can have but earth, which is his due;
74.8: My spirit is thine, the better part of me:
74.9: So then thou hast but lost the dregs of life,
74.10: The prey of worms, my body being dead,
74.11: The coward conquest of a wretch’s knife,
74.12: Too base of thee to be remembered.
74.13: The worth of that is that which it contains,
74.14: And that is this, and this with thee remains.
75.1: So are you to my thoughts as food to life,
75.2: Or as sweet-season’d showers are to the ground;
75.3: And for the peace of you I hold such strife
75.4: As ’twixt a miser and his wealth is found;
75.5: Now proud as an enjoyer and anon
75.6: Doubting the filching age will steal his treasure,
75.7: Now counting best to be with you alone,
75.8: Then better’d that the world may see my pleasure;
75.9: Sometime all full with feasting on your sight
75.10: And by and by clean starved for a look;
75.12: Save what is had or must from you be took.
75.13: Thus do I pine and surfeit day by day,
75.14: Or gluttoning on all, or all away.
76.1: Why is my verse so barren of new pride,
76.2: So far from variation or quick change?
76.3: Why with the time do I not glance aside
76.4: To new-found methods and to compounds strange?
76.5: Why write I still all one, ever the same,
76.6: And keep invention in a noted weed,
76.7: That every word doth almost tell my name,
76.8: Showing their birth and where they did proceed?
76.9: O, know, sweet love, I always write of you,
76.10: And you and love are still my argument;
76.11: So all my best is dressing old words new,
76.12: Spending again what is already spent:
76.13: For as the sun is daily new and old,
76.14: So is my love still telling what is told.
77.1: Thy glass will show thee how thy beauties wear,
77.2: Thy dial how thy precious minutes waste;
77.3: These vacant leaves thy mind’s imprint will bear,
77.4: And of this book this learning mayst thou taste.
77.5: The wrinkles which thy glass will truly show
77.6: Of mouthed graves will give thee memory;
77.7: Thou by thy dial’s shady stealth mayst know
77.9: Look, what thy memory cannot contain
77.10: Commit to these waste blanks, and thou shalt find
77.11: Those children nursed, deliver’d from thy brain,
77.12: To take a new acquaintance of thy mind.
77.13: These offices, so oft as thou wilt look,
77.14: Shall profit thee and much enrich thy book.
78.1: So oft have I invoked thee for my Muse
78.2: And found such fair assistance in my verse
78.3: As every alien pen hath got my use
78.4: And under thee their poesy disperse.
78.5: Thine eyes that taught the dumb on high to sing
78.6: And heavy ignorance aloft to fly
78.7: Have added feathers to the learned’s wing
78.8: And given grace a double majesty.
78.9: Yet be most proud of that which I compile,
78.10: Whose influence is thine and born of thee:
78.11: In others’ works thou dost but mend the style,
78.12: And arts with thy sweet graces graced be;
78.13: But thou art all my art and dost advance
78.14: As high as learning my rude ignorance.
79.1: Whilst I alone did call upon thy aid,
79.2: My verse alone had all thy gentle grace,
79.3: But now my gracious numbers are decay’d,
79.4: And my sick Muse doth give another place.
79.5: I grant, sweet love, thy lovely argument
79.6: Deserves the travail of a worthier pen,
79.7: Yet what of thee thy poet doth invent
79.8: He robs thee of and pays it thee again.
79.9: He lends thee virtue and he stole that word
79.10: From thy behaviour; beauty doth he give
79.11: And found it in thy cheek; he can afford
79.12: No praise to thee but what in thee doth live.
79.13: Then thank him not for that which he doth say,
79.14: Since what he owes thee thou thyself dost pay.
80.1: O, how I faint when I of you do write,
80.2: Knowing a better spirit doth use your name,
80.3: And in the praise thereof spends all his might,
80.4: To make me tongue-tied, speaking of your fame!
80.5: But since your worth, wide as the ocean is,
80.6: The humble as the proudest sail doth bear,
80.7: My saucy bark inferior far to his
80.8: On your broad main doth wilfully appear.
80.9: Your shallowest help will hold me up afloat,
80.10: Whilst he upon your soundless deep doth ride;
80.11: Or, being wreck’d, I am a worthless boat,
80.12: He of tall building and of goodly pride:
80.13: Then if he thrive and I be cast away,
80.14: The worst was this; my love was my decay.
81.1: Or I shall live your epitaph to make,
81.2: Or you survive when I in earth am rotten;
81.3: From hence your memory death cannot take,
81.4: Although in me each part will be forgotten.
81.5: Your name from hence immortal life shall have,
81.6: Though I, once gone, to all the world must die:
81.7: The earth can yield me but a common grave,
81.8: When you entombed in men’s eyes shall lie.
81.9: Your monument shall be my gentle verse,
81.10: Which eyes not yet created shall o’er-read,
81.11: And tongues to be your being shall rehearse
81.12: When all the breathers of this world are dead;
81.13: You still shall live⁠—such virtue hath my pen⁠—
81.14: Where breath most breathes, even in the mouths of men.
82.1: I grant thou wert not married to my Muse
82.2: And therefore mayst without attaint o’erlook
82.3: The dedicated words which writers use
82.4: Of their fair subject, blessing every book.
82.5: Thou art as fair in knowledge as in hue,
82.6: Finding thy worth a limit past my praise,
82.7: And therefore art enforced to seek anew
82.8: Some fresher stamp of the time-bettering days.
82.9: And do so, love; yet when they have devised
82.10: What strained touches rhetoric can lend,
82.11: Thou truly fair wert truly sympathized
82.12: In true plain words by thy true-telling friend;
82.13: And their gross painting might be better used
82.14: Where cheeks need blood; in thee it is abused.
83.1: I never saw that you did painting need
83.2: And therefore to your fair no painting set;
83.3: I found, or thought I found, you did exceed
83.4: That barren tender of a poet’s debt;
83.5: And therefore have I slept in your report,
83.6: That you yourself being extant well might show
83.7: How far a modern quill doth come too short,
83.8: Speaking of worth, what worth in you doth grow.
83.9: This silence for my sin you did impute,
83.10: Which shall be most my glory, being dumb;
83.11: For I impair not beauty being mute,
83.12: When others would give life and bring a tomb.
83.13: There lives more life in one of your fair eyes
83.14: Than both your poets can in praise devise.
84.1: Who is it that says most? which can say more
84.2: Than this rich praise, that you alone are you?
84.3: In whose confine immured is the store
84.4: Which should example where your equal grew.
84.5: Lean penury within that pen doth dwell
84.6: That to his subject lends not some small glory;
84.7: But he that writes of you, if he can tell
84.8: That you are you, so dignifies his story,
84.9: Let him but copy what in you is writ,
84.10: Not making worse what nature made so clear,
84.11: And such a counterpart shall fame his wit,
84.12: Making his style admired every where.
84.13: You to your beauteous blessings add a curse,
84.14: Being fond on praise, which makes your praises worse.
85.1: My tongue-tied Muse in manners holds her still,
85.2: While comments of your praise, richly compiled,
85.3: Reserve their character with golden quill
85.4: And precious phrase by all the Muses filed.
85.5: I think good thoughts whilst other write good words,
85.6: And like unletter’d clerk still cry “Amen”
85.7: To every hymn that able spirit affords
85.8: In polish’d form of well-refined pen.
85.9: Hearing you praised, I say “ ’Tis so, ’tis true,”
85.10: And to the most of praise add something more;
85.11: But that is in my thought, whose love to you,
85.12: Though words come hindmost, holds his rank before.
85.13: Then others for the breath of words respect,
85.14: Me for my dumb thoughts, speaking in effect.
86.1: Was it the proud full sail of his great verse,
86.2: Bound for the prize of all too precious you,
86.3: That did my ripe thoughts in my brain inhearse,
86.4: Making their tomb the womb wherein they grew?
86.5: Was it his spirit, by spirits taught to write
86.6: Above a mortal pitch, that struck me dead?
86.7: No, neither he, nor his compeers by night
86.8: Giving him aid, my verse astonished.
86.9: He, nor that affable familiar ghost
86.10: Which nightly gulls him with intelligence,
86.11: As victors of my silence cannot boast;
86.12: I was not sick of any fear from thence:
86.13: But when your countenance fill’d up his line,
86.14: Then lack’d I matter; that enfeebled mine.
87.1: Farewell! thou art too dear for my possessing,
87.2: And like enough thou know’st thy estimate:
87.3: The charter of thy worth gives thee releasing;
87.4: My bonds in thee are all determinate.
87.5: For how do I hold thee but by thy granting?
87.6: And for that riches where is my deserving?
87.7: The cause of this fair gift in me is wanting,
87.8: And so my patent back again is swerving.
87.9: Thyself thou gavest, thy own worth then not knowing,
87.10: Or me, to whom thou gavest it, else mistaking;
87.11: So thy great gift, upon misprision growing,
87.12: Comes home again, on better judgement making.
87.13: Thus have I had thee, as a dream doth flatter,
87.14: In sleep a king, but waking no such matter.
88.1: When thou shalt be disposed to set me light
88.2: And place my merit in the eye of scorn,
88.3: Upon thy side against myself I’ll fight
88.4: And prove thee virtuous, though thou art forsworn.
88.5: With mine own weakness being best acquainted,
88.6: Upon thy part I can set down a story
88.7: Of faults conceal’d, wherein I am attainted,
88.8: That thou in losing me shalt win much glory:
88.9: And I by this will be a gainer too;
88.10: For bending all my loving thoughts on thee,
88.11: The injuries that to myself I do,
88.13: Such is my love, to thee I so belong,
88.14: That for thy right myself will bear all wrong.
89.1: Say that thou didst forsake me for some fault,
89.2: And I will comment upon that offence;
89.3: Speak of my lameness, and I straight will halt,
89.4: Against thy reasons making no defence.
89.5: Thou canst not, love, disgrace me half so ill,
89.6: To set a form upon desired change,
89.7: As I’ll myself disgrace: knowing thy will,
89.8: I will acquaintance strangle and look strange,
89.9: Be absent from thy walks, and in my tongue
89.10: Thy sweet beloved name no more shall dwell,
89.11: Lest I, too much profane, should do it wrong
89.12: And haply of our old acquaintance tell.
89.13: For thee against myself I’ll vow debate,
89.14: For I must ne’er love him whom thou dost hate.
90.1: Then hate me when thou wilt; if ever, now;
90.2: Now, while the world is bent my deeds to cross,
90.3: Join with the spite of fortune, make me bow,
90.4: And do not drop in for an after-loss:
90.5: Ah, do not, when my heart hath ’scaped this sorrow,
90.6: Come in the rearward of a conquer’d woe;
90.7: Give not a windy night a rainy morrow,
90.8: To linger out a purposed overthrow.
90.9: If thou wilt leave me, do not leave me last,
90.10: When other petty griefs have done their spite,
90.11: But in the onset come; so shall I taste
90.12: At first the very worst of fortune’s might,
90.13: And other strains of woe, which now seem woe,
90.14: Compared with loss of thee will not seem so.
91.1: Some glory in their birth, some in their skill,
91.2: Some in their wealth, some in their body’s force,
91.3: Some in their garments, though new-fangled ill,
91.4: Some in their hawks and hounds, some in their horse;
91.5: And every humour hath his adjunct pleasure,
91.6: Wherein it finds a joy above the rest:
91.7: But these particulars are not my measure;
91.8: All these I better in one general best.
91.9: Thy love is better than high birth to me,
91.10: Richer than wealth, prouder than garments’ cost,
91.11: Of more delight than hawks and horses be;
91.12: And having thee, of all men’s pride I boast:
91.13: Wretched in this alone, that thou mayst take
91.14: All this away and me most wretchcd make.
92.1: But do thy worst to steal thyself away,
92.2: For term of life thou art assured mine,
92.3: And life no longer than thy love will stay,
92.4: For it depends upon that love of thine.
92.5: Then need I not to fear the worst of wrongs,
92.6: When in the least of them my life hath end.
92.7: I see a better state to me belongs
92.8: Than that which on thy humour doth depend;
92.9: Thou canst not vex me with inconstant mind,
92.10: Since that my life on thy revolt doth lie.
92.11: O, what a happy title do I find,
92.12: Happy to have thy love, happy to die!
92.13: But what’s so blessed-fair that fears no blot?
92.14: Thou mayst be false, and yet I know it not.
93.1: So shall I live, supposing thou art true,
93.2: Like a deceived husband; so love’s face
93.3: May still seem love to me, though alter’d new;
93.4: Thy looks with me, thy heart in other place:
93.5: For there can live no hatred in thine eye,
93.6: Therefore in that I cannot know thy change.
93.7: In many’s looks the false heart’s history
93.8: Is writ in moods and frowns and wrinkles strange,
93.9: But heaven in thy creation did decree
93.10: That in thy face sweet love should ever dwell;
93.11: Whate’er thy thoughts or thy heart’s workings be,
93.12: Thy looks should nothing thence but sweetness tell.
93.13: How like Eve’s apple doth thy beauty grow,
93.14: If thy sweet virtue answer not thy show!
94.1: They that have power to hurt and will do none,
94.2: That do not do the thing they most do show,
94.3: Who, moving others, are themselves as stone,
94.4: Unmoved, cold, and to temptation slow,
94.5: They rightly do inherit heaven’s graces
94.6: And husband nature’s riches from expense;
94.7: They are the lords and owners of their faces,
94.8: Others but stewards of their excellence.
94.9: The summer’s flower is to the summer sweet,
94.10: Though to itself it only live and die,
94.11: But if that flower with base infection meet,
94.12: The basest weed outbraves his dignity:
94.13: For sweetest things turn sourest by their deeds;
94.14: Lilies that fester smell far worse than weeds.
95.1: How sweet and lovely dost thou make the shame
95.2: Which, like a canker in the fragrant rose,
95.3: Doth spot the beauty of thy budding name!
95.4: O, in what sweets dost thou thy sins enclose!
95.5: That tongue that tells the story of thy days,
95.6: Making lascivious comments on thy sport,
95.7: Cannot dispraise but in a kind of praise;
95.8: Naming thy name blesses an ill report.
95.9: O, what a mansion have those vices got
95.10: Which for their habitation chose out thee,
95.11: Where beauty’s veil doth cover every blot,
95.12: And all things turns to fair that eyes can see!
95.13: Take heed, dear heart, of this large privilege;
95.14: The hardest knife ill-used doth lose his edge.
96.1: Some say thy fault is youth, some wantonness;
96.2: Some say thy grace is youth and gentle sport;
96.3: Both grace and faults are loved of more and less;
96.4: Thou makest faults graces that to thee resort.
96.5: As on the finger of a throned queen
96.6: The basest jewel will be well esteem’d,
96.7: So are those errors that in thee are seen
96.8: To truths translated and for true things deem’d.
96.9: How many lambs might the stern wolf betray,
96.10: If like a lamb he could his looks translate!
96.11: How many gazers mightst thou lead away,
96.12: If thou wouldst use the strength of all thy state!
96.13: But do not so; I love thee in such sort
96.14: As, thou being mine, mine is thy good report.
97.1: How like a winter hath my absence been
97.2: From thee, the pleasure of the fleeting year!
97.3: What freezings have I felt, what dark days seen!
97.5: And yet this time removed was summer’s time,
97.6: The teeming autumn, big with rich increase,
97.7: Bearing the wanton burthen of the prime,
97.8: Like widow’d wombs after their lords’ decease:
97.9: Yet this abundant issue seem’d to me
97.10: But hope of orphans and unfather’d fruit;
97.11: For summer and his pleasures wait on thee,
97.12: And, thou away, the very birds are mute;
97.13: Or, if they sing, ’tis with so dull a cheer
97.14: That leaves look pale, dreading the winter’s near.
98.1: From you have I been absent in the spring,
98.2: When proud-pied April dress’d in all his trim
98.3: Hath put a spirit of youth in everything,
98.4: That heavy Saturn laugh’d and leap’d with him.
98.5: Yet nor the lays of birds nor the sweet smell
98.6: Of different flowers in odour and in hue
98.7: Could make me any summer’s story tell,
98.8: Or from their proud lap pluck them where they grew;
98.9: Nor did I wonder at the lily’s white,
98.10: Nor praise the deep vermilion in the rose;
98.11: They were but sweet, but figures of delight,
98.12: Drawn after you, you pattern of all those.
98.13: Yet seem’d it winter still, and, you away,
98.14: As with your shadow I with these did play:
99.1: The forward violet thus did I chide:
99.2: Sweet thief, whence didst thou steal thy sweet that smells,
99.3: If not from my love’s breath? The purple pride
99.4: Which on thy soft cheek for complexion dwells
99.5: In my love’s veins thou hast too grossly dyed.
99.6: The lily I condemned for thy hand,
99.7: And buds of marjoram had stol’n thy hair:
99.8: The roses fearfully on thorns did stand,
99.9: One blushing shame, another white despair;
99.10: A third, nor red nor white, had stol’n of both
99.11: And to his robbery had annex’d thy breath;
99.12: But, for his theft, in pride of all his growth
99.13: A vengeful canker eat him up to death.
99.14: More flowers I noted, yet I none could see
99.15: But sweet or colour it had stol’n from thee.
100.1: Where art thou, Muse, that thou forget’st so long
100.2: To speak of that which gives thee all thy might?
100.3: Spend’st thou thy fury on some worthless song,
100.4: Darkening thy power to lend base subjects light?
100.5: Return forgetful Muse, and straight redeem
100.6: In gentle numbers time so idly spent;
100.7: Sing to the ear that doth thy lays esteem
100.8: And gives thy pen both skill and argument.
100.9: Rise, resty Muse, my love’s sweet face survey,
100.10: If Time have any wrinkle graven there;
100.11: If any, be a satire to decay,
100.12: And make Time’s spoils despised everywhere.
100.13: Give my love fame faster than Time wastes life;
100.14: So thou prevent’st his scythe and crooked knife.
101.1: O truant Muse, what shall be thy amends
101.2: For thy neglect of truth in beauty dyed?
101.3: Both truth and beauty on my love depends;
101.4: So dost thou too, and therein dignified.
101.5: Make answer, Muse: wilt thou not haply say
101.6: “Truth needs no colour, with his colour fix’d;
101.7: Beauty no pencil, beauty’s truth to lay;
101.8: But best is best, if never intermix’d?”
101.9: Because he needs no praise, wilt thou be dumb?
101.10: Excuse not silence so; for’t lies in thee
101.11: To make him much outlive a gilded tomb,
101.12: And to be praised of ages yet to be.
101.13: Then do thy office, Muse; I teach thee how
101.14: To make him seem long hence as he shows now.
102.1: My love is strengthen’d, though more weak in seeming;
102.2: I love not less, though less the show appear:
102.3: That love is merchandized whose rich esteeming
102.4: The owner’s tongue doth publish every where.
102.5: Our love was new and then but in the spring
102.6: When I was wont to greet it with my lays,
102.7: As Philomel in summer’s front doth sing
102.8: And stops her pipe in growth of riper days:
102.9: Not that the summer is less pleasant now
102.10: Than when her mournful hymns did hush the night,
102.11: But that wild music burthens every bough
102.12: And sweets grown common lose their dear delight.
102.13: Therefore like her I sometime hold my tongue,
102.14: Because I would not dull you with my song.
103.1: Alack, what poverty my Muse brings forth,
103.2: That having such a scope to show her pride,
103.3: The argument all bare is of more worth
103.4: Than when it hath my added praise beside!
103.5: O, blame me not, if I no more can write!
103.6: Look in your glass, and there appears a face
103.7: That over-goes my blunt invention quite,
103.8: Dulling my lines and doing me disgrace.
103.9: Were it not sinful then, striving to mend,
103.10: To mar the subject that before was well?
103.11: For to no other pass my verses tend
103.12: Than of your graces and your gifts to tell;
103.13: And more, much more, than in my verse can sit
103.14: Your own glass shows you when you look in it.
104.1: To me, fair friend, you never can be old,
104.2: For as you were when first your eye I eyed,
104.3: Such seems your beauty still. Three winters cold,
104.4: Have from the forests shook three summers’ pride,
104.5: Three beauteous springs to yellow autumn turn’d
104.6: In process of the seasons have I seen,
104.7: Three April perfumes in three hot Junes burn’d,
104.8: Since first I saw you fresh, which yet are green.
104.9: Ah! yet doth beauty, like a dial-hand,
104.10: Steal from his figure and no pace perceived;
104.11: So your sweet hue, which methinks still doth stand,
104.12: Hath motion and mine eye may be deceived:
104.13: For fear of which, hear this, thou age unbred;
104.14: Ere you were born was beauty’s summer dead.
105.1: Let not my love be call’d idolatry,
105.2: Nor my beloved as an idol show,
105.3: Since all alike my songs and praises be
105.4: To one, of one, still such, and ever so.
105.5: Kind is my love to-day, to-morrow kind,
105.6: Still constant in a wondrous excellence;
105.7: Therefore my verse to constancy confined,
105.8: One thing expressing, leaves out difference.
105.9: “Fair, kind, and true” is all my argument,
105.10: “Fair, kind, and true” varying to other words;
105.11: And in this change is my invention spent,
105.12: Three themes in one, which wondrous scope affords.
105.13: “Fair, kind, and true,” have often lived alone,
105.14: Which three till now never kept seat in one.
106.1: When in the chronicle of wasted time
106.2: I see descriptions of the fairest wights,
106.3: And beauty making beautiful old rhyme
106.4: In praise of ladies dead and lovely knights,
106.5: Then, in the blazon of sweet beauty’s best,
106.6: Of hand, of foot, of lip, of eye, of brow,
106.7: I see their antique pen would have express’d
106.8: Even such a beauty as you master now.
106.9: So all their praises are but prophecies
106.10: Of this our time, all you prefiguring;
106.11: And, for they look’d but with divining eyes,
106.12: They had not skill enough your worth to sing:
106.13: For we, which now behold these present days,
106.14: Have eyes to wonder, but lack tongues to praise.
107.1: Not mine own fears, nor the prophetic soul
107.2: Of the wide world dreaming on things to come,
107.3: Can yet the lease of my true love control,
107.4: Supposed as forfeit to a confined doom.
107.5: The mortal moon hath her eclipse endured
107.6: And the sad augurs mock their own presage;
107.8: And peace proclaims olives of endless age.
107.9: Now with the drops of this most balmy time
107.10: My love looks fresh, and Death to me subscribes,
107.11: Since, spite of him, I’ll live in this poor rhyme,
107.12: While he insults o’er dull and speechless tribes:
107.13: And thou in this shalt find thy monument,
107.14: When tyrants’ crests and tombs of brass are spent.
108.1: What’s in the brain that ink may character
108.2: Which hath not figured to thee my true spirit?
108.3: What’s new to speak, what now to register,
108.4: That may express my love or thy dear merit?
108.5: Nothing, sweet boy; but yet, like prayers divine,
108.6: I must each day say o’er the very same,
108.7: Counting no old thing old, thou mine, I thine,
108.8: Even as when first I hallow’d thy fair name.
108.9: So that eternal love in love’s fresh case
108.10: Weighs not the dust and injury of age,
108.11: Nor gives to necessary wrinkles place,
108.12: But makes antiquity for aye his page,
108.13: Finding the first conceit of love there bred
108.14: Where time and outward form would show it dead.
109.1: O, never say that I was false of heart,
109.2: Though absence seem’d my flame to qualify.
109.3: As easy might I from myself depart
109.4: As from my soul, which in thy breast doth lie:
109.5: That is my home of love: if I have ranged,
109.6: Like him that travels I return again,
109.7: Just to the time, not with the time exchanged,
109.8: So that myself bring water for my stain.
109.9: Never believe, though in my nature reign’d
109.10: All frailties that besiege all kinds of blood,
109.11: That it could so preposterously be stain’d,
109.12: To leave for nothing all thy sum of good;
109.13: For nothing this wide universe I call,
109.14: Save thou, my rose; in it thou art my all.
110.1: Alas, ’tis true I have gone here and there
110.2: And made myself a motley to the view,
110.3: Gored mine own thoughts, sold cheap what is most dear,
110.4: Made old offences of affections new;
110.5: Most true it is that I have look’d on truth
110.6: Askance and strangely: but, by all above,
110.7: These blenches gave my heart another youth,
110.8: And worse essays proved thee my best of love.
110.9: Now all is done, have what shall have no end:
110.10: Mine appetite I never more will grind
110.11: On newer proof, to try an older friend,
110.12: A god in love, to whom I am confined.
110.13: Then give me welcome, next my heaven the best,
110.14: Even to thy pure and most most loving breast.
111.1: O, for my sake do you with Fortune chide,
111.2: The guilty goddess of my harmful deeds,
111.3: That did not better for my life provide
111.4: Than public means which public manners breeds.
111.5: Thence comes it that my name receives a brand,
111.6: And almost thence my nature is subdued
111.7: To what it works in, like the dyer’s hand:
111.8: Pity me then and wish I were renew’d;
111.9: Whilst, like a willing patient, I will drink
111.10: Potions of eisel ’gainst my strong infection;
111.11: No bitterness that I will bitter think,
111.12: Nor double penance, to correct correction.
111.13: Pity me then, dear friend, and I assure ye
111.14: Even that your pity is enough to cure me.
112.1: Your love and pity doth the impression fill
112.2: Which vulgar scandal stamp’d upon my brow;
112.3: For what care I who calls me well or ill,
112.4: So you o’er-green my bad, my good allow?
112.5: You are my all the world, and I must strive
112.6: To know my shames and praises from your tongue;
112.7: None else to me, nor I to none alive,
112.8: That my steel’d sense or changes right or wrong.
112.9: In so profound abysm I throw all care
112.10: Of others’ voices, that my adder’s sense
112.11: To critic and to flatterer stopped are.
112.12: Mark how with my neglect I do dispense:
112.13: You are so strongly in my purpose bred
112.14: That all the world besides methinks are dead.
113.1: Since I left you, mine eye is in my mind;
113.2: And that which governs me to go about
113.3: Doth part his function and is partly blind,
113.4: Seems seeing, but effectually is out;
113.5: For it no form delivers to the heart
113.6: Of bird, of flower, or shape, which it doth latch:
113.7: Of his quick objects hath the mind no part,
113.8: Nor his own vision holds what it doth catch;
113.9: For if it see the rudest or gentlest sight,
113.10: The most sweet favour or deformed’st creature,
113.11: The mountain or the sea, the day or night,
113.12: The crow or dove, it shapes them to your feature:
113.13: Incapable of more, replete with you,
113.14: My most true mind thus makes mine untrue.
114.1: Or whether doth my mind, being crown’d with you,
114.2: Drink up the monarch’s plague, this flattery?
114.3: Or whether shall I say, mine eye saith true,
114.4: And that your love taught it this alchemy,
114.5: To make of monsters and things indigest
114.6: Such cherubins as your sweet self resemble,
114.7: Creating every bad a perfect best,
114.8: As fast as objects to his beams assemble?
114.9: O, ’tis the first; ’tis flattery in my seeing,
114.10: And my great mind most kingly drinks it up:
114.11: Mine eye well knows what with his gust is ’greeing,
114.12: And to his palate doth prepare the cup:
114.13: If it be poison’d, ’tis the lesser sin
114.14: That mine eye loves it and doth first begin.
115.1: Those lines that I before have writ do lie,
115.2: Even those that said I could not love you dearer:
115.3: Yet then my judgment knew no reason why
115.4: My most full flame should afterwards burn clearer.
115.5: But reckoning time, whose million’d accidents
115.6: Creep in ’twixt vows and change decrees of kings,
115.7: Tan sacred beauty, blunt the sharp’st intents,
115.8: Divert strong minds to the course of altering things;
115.9: Alas, why, fearing of time’s tyranny,
115.10: Might I not then say “Now I love you best,”
115.11: When I was certain o’er incertainty,
115.12: Crowning the present, doubting of the rest?
115.13: Love is a babe; then might I not say so,
115.14: To give full growth to that which still doth grow?
116.1: Let me not to the marriage of true minds
116.2: Admit impediments. Love is not love
116.3: Which alters when it alteration finds,
116.4: Or bends with the remover to remove:
116.5: O, no! it is an ever-fixed mark
116.6: That looks on tempests and is never shaken;
116.7: It is the star to every wandering bark,
116.8: Whose worth’s unknown, although his height be taken.
116.9: Love’s not Time’s fool, though rosy lips and cheeks
116.10: Within his bending sickle’s compass come;
116.11: Love alters not with his brief hours and weeks,
116.12: But bears it out even to the edge of doom.
116.13: If this be error and upon me proved,
116.14: I never writ, nor no man ever loved.
117.1: Accuse me thus: that I have scanted all
117.2: Wherein I should your great deserts repay,
117.3: Forgot upon your dearest love to call,
117.4: Whereto all bonds do tie me day by day;
117.5: That I have frequent been with unknown minds
117.6: And given to time your own dear-purchased right;
117.7: That I have hoisted sail to all the winds
117.8: Which should transport me farthest from your sight.
117.9: Book both my wilfulness and errors down
117.10: And on just proof surmise accumulate;
117.11: Bring me within the level of your frown,
117.12: But shoot not at me in your waken’d hate;
117.13: Since my appeal says I did strive to prove
117.14: The constancy and virtue of your love.
118.1: Like as, to make our appetite more keen,
118.2: With eager compounds we our palate urge,
118.3: As, to prevent our maladies unseen,
118.4: We sicken to shun sickness when we purge,
118.5: Even so, being full of your ne’er-cloying sweetness,
118.6: To bitter sauces did I frame my feeding
118.7: And, sick of welfare, found a kind of meetness
118.8: To be diseased ere that there was true needing.
118.9: Thus policy in love, to anticipate
118.10: The ills that were not, grew to faults assured
118.11: And brought to medicine a healthful state
118.12: Which, rank of goodness, would by ill be cured:
118.13: But thence I learn, and find the lesson true,
118.14: Drugs poison him that so fell sick of you.
119.1: What potions have I drunk of Siren tears,
119.2: Distill’d from limbecks foul as hell within,
119.3: Applying fears to hopes and hopes to fears,
119.4: Still losing when I saw myself to win!
119.5: What wretched errors hath my heart committed,
119.6: Whilst it hath thought itself so blessed never!
119.7: How have mine eyes out of their spheres been fitted
119.8: In the distraction of this madding fever!
119.9: O benefit of ill! now I find true
119.10: That better is by evil still made better;
119.11: And ruin’d love, when it is built anew,
119.12: Grows fairer than at first, more strong, far greater.
119.13: So I return rebuked to my content
119.14: And gain by ills thrice more than I have spent.
120.1: That you were once unkind befriends me now,
120.2: And for that sorrow which I then did feel
120.3: Needs must I under my transgression bow,
120.4: Unless my nerves were brass or hammer’d steel.
120.5: For if you were by my unkindness shaken
120.6: As I by yours, you’ve pass’d a hell of time,
120.7: And I, a tyrant, have no leisure taken
120.8: To weigh how once I suffer’d in your crime.
120.9: O, that our night of woe might have remember’d
120.10: My deepest sense, how hard true sorrow hits,
120.11: And soon to you, as you to me, then tender’d
120.12: The humble salve which wounded bosoms fits!
120.13: But that your trespass now becomes a fee;
120.14: Mine ransoms yours, and yours must ransom me.
121.1: ’Tis better to be vile than vile esteem’d,
121.2: When not to be receives reproach of being,
121.3: And the just pleasure lost which is so deem’d
121.4: Not by our feeling but by others’ seeing:
121.5: For why should others’ false adulterate eyes
121.6: Give salutation to my sportive blood?
121.7: Or on my frailties why are frailer spies,
121.8: Which in their wills count bad what I think good?
121.9: No, I am that I am, and they that level
121.10: At my abuses reckon up their own:
121.11: I may be straight, though they themselves be bevel;
121.12: By their rank thoughts my deeds must not be shown;
121.13: Unless this general evil they maintain,
121.14: All men are bad, and in their badness reign.
122.1: Thy gift, thy tables, are within my brain
122.3: Which shall above that idle rank remain
122.4: Beyond all date, even to eternity;
122.5: Or at the least, so long as brain and heart
122.6: Have faculty by nature to subsist;
122.7: Till each to razed oblivion yield his part
122.8: Of thee, thy record never can be miss’d.
122.9: That poor retention could not so much hold,
122.10: Nor need I tallies thy dear love to score;
122.11: Therefore to give them from me was I bold,
122.12: To trust those tables that receive thee more:
122.13: To keep an adjunct to remember thee
122.14: Were to import forgetfulness in me.
123.1: No, Time, thou shalt not boast that I do change:
123.2: Thy pyramids built up with newer might
123.3: To me are nothing novel, nothing strange;
123.4: They are but dressings of a former sight.
123.5: Our dates are brief, and therefore we admire
123.6: What thou dost foist upon us that is old,
123.7: And rather make them born to our desire
123.8: Than think that we before have heard them told:
123.9: Thy registers and thee I both defy,
123.10: Not wondering at the present nor the past,
123.11: For thy records and what we see doth lie,
123.12: Made more or less by thy continual haste.
123.13: This I do vow and this shall ever be;
123.14: I will be true, despite thy scythe and thee.
124.1: If my dear love were but the child of state,
124.2: It might for Fortune’s bastard be unfather’d,
124.3: As subject to Time’s love or to Time’s hate,
124.4: Weeds among weeds, or flowers with flowers gather’d.
124.5: No, it was builded far from accident;
124.6: It suffers not in smiling pomp, nor falls
124.7: Under the blow of thralled discontent,
124.8: Whereto the inviting time our fashion calls:
124.9: It fears not policy, that heretic,
124.10: Which works on leases of short-number’d hours,
124.11: But all alone stands hugely politic,
124.12: That it nor grows with heat nor drowns with showers.
124.13: To this I witness call the fools of time,
124.14: Which die for goodness, who have lived for crime.
125.1: Were’t aught to me I bore the canopy,
125.2: With my extern the outward honouring,
125.3: Or laid great bases for eternity,
125.4: Which prove more short than waste or ruining?
125.5: Have I not seen dwellers on form and favour
125.6: Lose all, and more, by paying too much rent,
125.7: For compound sweet forgoing simple savour,
125.8: Pitiful thrivers, in their gazing spent?
125.9: No, let me be obsequious in thy heart,
125.10: And take thou my oblation, poor but free,
125.11: Which is not mix’d with seconds, knows no art,
125.12: But mutual render, only me for thee.
125.13: Hence, thou suborn’d informer! a true soul
125.14: When most impeach’d stands least in thy control.
126.1: O thou, my lovely boy, who in thy power
126.2: Dost hold Time’s fickle glass, his sickle, hour;
126.3: Who hast by waning grown, and therein show’st
126.4: Thy lovers withering as thy sweet self grow’st;
126.5: If Nature, sovereign mistress over wrack,
126.6: As thou goest onwards, still will pluck thee back,
126.7: She keeps thee to this purpose, that her skill
126.8: May time disgrace and wretched minutes kill.
126.9: Yet fear her, O thou minion of her pleasure!
126.10: She may detain, but not still keep, her treasure:
126.11: Her audit, though delay’d, answer’d must be,
126.12: And her quietus is to render thee.
127.1: In the old age black was not counted fair,
127.2: Or if it were, it bore not beauty’s name;
127.3: But now is black beauty’s successive heir,
127.4: And beauty slander’d with a bastard shame:
127.5: For since each hand hath put on nature’s power,
127.6: Fairing the foul with art’s false borrow’d face,
127.7: Sweet beauty hath no name, no holy bower,
127.8: But is profaned, if not lives in disgrace.
127.9: Therefore my mistress’ brows are raven black,
127.10: Her eyes so suited, and they mourners seem
127.11: At such who, not born fair, no beauty lack,
127.12: Slandering creation with a false esteem:
127.13: Yet so they mourn, becoming of their woe,
127.14: That every tongue says beauty should look so.
128.1: How oft, when thou, my music, music play’st,
128.2: Upon that blessed wood whose motion sounds
128.3: With thy sweet fingers, when thou gently sway’st
128.4: The wiry concord that mine ear confounds,
128.5: Do I envy those jacks that nimble leap
128.6: To kiss the tender inward of thy hand,
128.7: Whilst my poor lips, which should that harvest reap,
128.8: At the wood’s boldness by thee blushing stand!
128.9: To be so tickled, they would change their state
128.10: And situation with those dancing chips,
128.11: O’er whom thy fingers walk with gentle gait,
128.12: Making dead wood more blest than living lips.
128.13: Since saucy jacks so happy are in this,
128.14: Give them thy fingers, me thy lips to kiss.
129.1: The expense of spirit in a waste of shame
129.2: Is lust in action; and till action, lust
129.3: Is perjured, murderous, bloody, full of blame,
129.4: Savage, extreme, rude, cruel, not to trust,
129.5: Enjoy’d no sooner but despised straight,
129.6: Past reason hunted, and no sooner had
129.7: Past reason hated, as a swallow’d bait
129.8: On purpose laid to make the taker mad;
129.9: Mad in pursuit and in possession so;
129.10: Had, having, and in quest to have, extreme;
129.11: A bliss in proof, and proved, a very woe;
129.12: Before, a joy proposed; behind a dream.
129.13: All this the world well knows; yet none knows well
129.14: To shun the heaven that leads men to this hell.
130.1: My mistress’ eyes are nothing like the sun;
130.2: Coral is far more red than her lips’ red;
130.3: If snow be white, why then her breasts are dun;
130.4: If hairs be wires, black wires grow on her head.
130.5: I have seen roses damask’d, red and white,
130.6: But no such roses see I in her cheeks;
130.7: And in some perfumes is there more delight
130.8: Than in the breath that from my mistress reeks.
130.9: I love to hear her speak, yet well I know
130.10: That music hath a far more pleasing sound;
130.11: I grant I never saw a goddess go;
130.12: My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground:
130.13: And yet, by heaven, I think my love as rare
130.14: As any she belied with false compare.
131.1: Thou art as tyrannous, so as thou art,
131.2: As those whose beauties proudly make them cruel;
131.3: For well thou know’st to my dear doting heart
131.4: Thou art the fairest and most precious jewel.
131.5: Yet, in good faith, some say that thee behold
131.6: Thy face hath not the power to make love groan:
131.7: To say they err I dare not be so bold,
131.8: Although I swear it to myself alone.
131.9: And, to be sure that is not false I swear,
131.10: A thousand groans, but thinking on thy face,
131.11: One on another’s neck, do witness bear
131.12: Thy black is fairest in my judgment’s place.
131.13: In nothing art thou black save in thy deeds,
131.14: And thence this slander, as I think, proceeds.
132.1: Thine eyes I love, and they, as pitying me,
132.2: Knowing thy heart torment me with disdain,
132.3: Have put on black and loving mourners be,
132.4: Looking with pretty ruth upon my pain.
132.5: And truly not the morning sun of heaven
132.6: Better becomes the grey cheeks of the east,
132.7: Nor that full star that ushers in the even
132.8: Doth half that glory to the sober west,
132.9: As those two mourning eyes become thy face:
132.10: O, let it then as well beseem thy heart
132.11: To mourn for me, since mourning doth thee grace,
132.12: And suit thy pity like in every part.
132.13: Then will I swear beauty herself is black
132.14: And all they foul that thy complexion lack.
133.1: Beshrew that heart that makes my heart to groan
133.2: For that deep wound it gives my friend and me!
133.3: Is’t not enough to torture me alone,
133.4: But slave to slavery my sweet’st friend must be?
133.5: Me from myself thy cruel eye hath taken,
133.6: And my next self thou harder hast engross’d:
133.7: Of him, myself, and thee, I am forsaken;
133.8: A torment thrice threefold thus to be cross’d.
133.9: Prison my heart in thy steel bosom’s ward,
133.10: But then my friend’s heart let my poor heart bail;
133.11: Whoe’er keeps me, let my heart be his guard;
133.12: Thou canst not then use rigour in my gaol:
133.13: And yet thou wilt; for I, being pent in thee,
133.14: Perforce am thine, and all that is in me.
134.1: So, now I have confess’d that he is thine,
134.2: And I myself am mortgaged to thy will,
134.3: Myself I’ll forfeit, so that other mine
134.4: Thou wilt restore, to be my comfort still:
134.5: But thou wilt not, nor he will not be free,
134.6: For thou art covetous and he is kind;
134.7: He learn’d but surety-like to write for me
134.8: Under that bond that him as fist doth bind.
134.9: The statute of thy beauty thou wilt take,
134.10: Thou usurer, that put’st forth all to use,
134.11: And sue a friend came debtor for my sake;
134.12: So him I lose through my unkind abuse.
134.13: Him have I lost; thou hast both him and me:
134.14: He pays the whole, and yet am I not free.
135.1: Whoever hath her wish, thou hast thy “Will,”
135.2: And “Will” to boot, and “Will” in overplus;
135.3: More than enough am I that vex thee still,
135.4: To thy sweet will making addition thus.
135.5: Wilt thou, whose will is large and spacious,
135.6: Not once vouchsafe to hide my will in thine?
135.7: Shall will in others seem right gracious,
135.8: And in my will no fair acceptance shine?
135.9: The sea, all water, yet receives rain still
135.10: And in abundance addeth to his store;
135.11: So thou, being rich in “Will,” add to thy “Will”
135.12: One will of mine, to make thy large “Will” more.
135.13: Let no unkind, no fair beseechers kill;
135.14: Think all but one, and me in that one “Will.”
136.1: If thy soul check thee that I come so near,
136.2: Swear to thy blind soul that I was thy “Will,”
136.3: And will, thy soul knows, is admitted there;
136.4: Thus far for love my love-suit, sweet, fulfil.
136.5: “Will” will fulfil the treasure of thy love,
136.6: Ay, fill it full with wills, and my will one.
136.7: In things of great receipt with case we prove
136.8: Among a number one is reckon’d none:
136.9: Then in the number let me pass untold,
136.10: Though in thy stores’ account I one must be;
136.11: For nothing hold me, so it please thee hold
136.12: That nothing me, a something sweet to thee:
136.13: Make but my name thy love, and love that still,
136.14: And then thou lovest me, for my name is “Will.”
137.1: Thou blind fool, Love, what dost thou to mine eyes,
137.2: That they behold, and see not what they see?
137.3: They know what beauty is, see where it lies,
137.4: Yet what the best is take the worst to be.
137.5: If eyes corrupt by over-partial looks
137.6: Be anchor’d in the bay where all men ride,
137.7: Why of eyes’ falsehood hast thou forged hooks,
137.8: Whereto the judgment of my heart is tied?
137.9: Why should my heart think that a several plot
137.10: Which my heart knows the wide world’s common place?
137.11: Or mine eyes seeing this, say this is not,
137.12: To put fair truth upon so foul a face?
137.13: In things right true my heart and eyes have erred,
137.14: And to this false plague are they now transferr’d.
138.1: When my love swears that she is made of truth
138.2: I do believe her, though I know she lies,
138.3: That she might think me some untutor’d youth,
138.4: Unlearned in the world’s false subtleties.
138.5: Thus vainly thinking that she thinks me young,
138.6: Although she knows my days are past the best,
138.7: Simply I credit her false-speaking tongue:
138.8: On both sides thus is simple truth suppress’d.
138.9: But wherefore says she not she is unjust?
138.10: And wherefore say not I that I am old?
138.11: O, love’s best habit is in seeming trust,
138.12: And age in love loves not to have years told:
138.13: Therefore I lie with her and she with me,
138.14: And in our faults by lies we flatter’d be.
139.1: O, call not me to justify the wrong
139.2: That thy unkindness lays upon my heart;
139.3: Wound me not with thine eye but with thy tongue;
139.4: Use power with power and slay me not by art.
139.5: Tell me thou lovest elsewhere, but in my sight,
139.6: Dear heart, forbear to glance thine eye aside:
139.7: What need’st thou wound with cunning when thy might
139.8: Is more than my o’er-press’d defence can bide?
139.9: Let me excuse thee: ah! my love well knows
139.10: Her pretty looks have been mine enemies,
139.11: And therefore from my face she turns my foes,
139.12: That they elsewhere might dart their injuries:
139.13: Yet do not so; but since I am near slain,
139.14: Kill me outright with looks and rid my pain.
140.1: Be wise as thou art cruel; do not press
140.2: My tongue-tied patience with too much disdain;
140.3: Lest sorrow lend me words and words express
140.4: The manner of my pity-wanting pain.
140.5: If I might teach thee wit, better it were,
140.6: Though not to love, yet, love, to tell me so;
140.7: As testy sick men, when their deaths be near,
140.8: No news but health from their physicians know;
140.9: For if I should despair, I should grow mad,
140.10: And in my madness might speak ill of thee:
140.11: Now this ill-wresting world is grown so bad,
140.12: Mad slanderers by mad ears believed be.
140.13: That I may not be so, nor thou belied,
140.14: Bear thine eyes straight, though thy proud heart go wide.
141.1: In faith, I do not love thee with mine eyes,
141.2: For they in thee a thousand errors note;
141.3: But ’tis my heart that loves what they despise,
141.4: Who in despite of view is pleased to dote;
141.5: Nor are mine ears with thy tongue’s tune delighted,
141.6: Nor tender feeling, to base touches prone,
141.7: Nor taste, nor smell, desire to be invited
141.8: To any sensual feast with thee alone:
141.9: But my five wits nor my five senses can
141.10: Dissuade one foolish heart from serving thee,
141.11: Who leaves unsway’d the likeness of a man,
141.12: Thy proud heart’s slave and vassal wretch to be:
141.13: Only my plague thus far I count my gain,
141.14: That she that makes me sin awards me pain.
142.1: Love is my sin and thy dear virtue hate,
142.2: Hate of my sin, grounded on sinful loving:
142.3: O, but with mine compare thou thine own state,
142.4: And thou shalt find it merits not reproving;
142.5: Or, if it do, not from those lips of thine,
142.6: That have profaned their scarlet ornaments
142.7: And seal’d false bonds of love as oft as mine,
142.8: Robb’d others’ beds’ revenues of their rents.
142.9: Be it lawful I love thee, as thou lovest those
142.10: Whom thine eyes woo as mine importune thee:
142.11: Root pity in thy heart, that when it grows
142.12: Thy pity may deserve to pitied be.
142.13: If thou dost seek to have what thou dost hide,
142.14: By self-example mayst thou be denied!
143.1: Lo! as a careful housewife runs to catch
143.2: One of her feather’d creatures broke away,
143.3: Sets down her babe and makes all swift dispatch
143.4: In pursuit of the thing she would have stay,
143.5: Whilst her neglected child holds her in chase,
143.6: Cries to catch her whose busy care is bent
143.7: To follow that which flies before her face,
143.8: Not prizing her poor infant’s discontent;
143.9: So runn’st thou after that which flies from thee,
143.10: Whilst I thy babe chase thee afar behind;
143.11: But if thou catch thy hope, turn back to me,
143.12: And play the mother’s part, kiss me, be kind:
143.13: So will I pray that thou mayst have thy “Will,”
143.14: If thou turn back, and my loud crying still.
144.1: Two loves I have of comfort and despair,
144.2: Which like two spirits do suggest me still:
144.3: The better angel is a man right fair,
144.4: The worser spirit a woman colour’d ill.
144.5: To win me soon to hell, my female evil
144.6: Tempteth my better angel from my side,
144.7: And would corrupt my saint to be a devil,
144.8: Wooing his purity with her foul pride.
144.9: And whether that my angel be turn’d fiend
144.10: Suspect I may, yet not directly tell;
144.11: But being both from me, both to each friend,
144.12: I guess one angel in another’s hell:
144.13: Yet this shall I ne’er know, but live in doubt,
144.14: Till my bad angel fire my good one out.
145.1: Those lips that Love’s own hand did make
145.2: Breathed forth the sound that said “I hate”
145.3: To me that languish’d for her sake;
145.4: But when she saw my woeful state,
145.5: Straight in her heart did mercy come,
145.6: Chiding that tongue that ever sweet
145.7: Was used in giving gentle doom,
145.8: And taught it thus anew to greet;
145.9: “I hate” she alter’d with an end,
145.10: That follow’d it as gentle day
145.11: Doth follow night, who like a fiend
145.12: From heaven to hell is flown away;
145.13: “I hate” from hate away she threw,
145.14: And saved my life, saying “not you.”
146.1: Poor soul, the centre of my sinful earth,
146.2: Why feed’st these rebel powers that thee array,
146.3: Why dost thou pine within and suffer dearth,
146.4: Painting thy outward walls so costly gay?
146.5: Why so large cost, having so short a lease,
146.6: Dost thou upon thy fading mansion spend?
146.7: Shall worms, inheritors of this excess,
146.8: Eat up thy charge? is this thy body’s end?
146.9: Then, soul, live thou upon thy servant’s loss,
146.10: And let that pine to aggravate thy store;
146.11: Buy terms divine in selling hours of dross;
146.12: Within be fed, without be rich no more:
146.13: So shall thou feed on Death, that feeds on men,
146.14: And Death once dead, there’s no more dying then.
147.1: My love is as a fever, longing still
147.2: For that which longer nurseth the disease,
147.3: Feeding on that which doth preserve the ill,
147.4: The uncertain sickly appetite to please.
147.5: My reason, the physician to my love,
147.6: Angry that his prescriptions are not kept,
147.7: Hath left me, and I desperate now approve
147.8: Desire is death, which physic did except.
147.9: Past cure I am, now reason is past care,
147.11: My thoughts and my discourse as madmen’s are,
147.12: At random from the truth vainly express’d;
147.13: For I have sworn thee fair and thought thee bright,
147.14: Who art as black as hell, as dark as night.
148.1: O me, what eyes hath Love put in my head,
148.2: Which have no correspondence with true sight!
148.3: Or, if they have, where is my judgment fled,
148.4: That censures falsely what they see aright?
148.5: If that be fair whereon my false eyes dote,
148.6: What means the world to say it is not so?
148.7: If it be not, then love doth well denote
148.8: Love’s eye is not so true as all men’s “No.”
148.9: How can it? O, how can Love’s eye be true,
148.10: That is so vex’d with watching and with tears?
148.11: No marvel then, though I mistake my view;
148.12: The sun itself sees not till heaven clears.
148.13: O cunning Love! with tears thou keep’st me blind,
148.14: Lest eyes well-seeing thy foul faults should find.
149.1: Canst thou, O cruel! say I love thee not,
149.2: When I against myself with thee partake?
149.3: Do I not think on thee, when I forgot
149.4: Am of myself, all tyrant, for thy sake?
149.5: Who hateth thee that I do call my friend?
149.6: On whom frown’st thou that I do fawn upon?
149.7: Nay, if thou lour’st on me, do I not spend
149.8: Revenge upon myself with present moan?
149.9: What merit do I in myself respect,
149.10: That is so proud thy service to despise,
149.11: When all my best doth worship thy defect,
149.12: Commanded by the motion of thine eyes?
149.13: But, love, hate on, for now I know thy mind;
149.14: Those that can see thou lovest, and I am blind.
150.1: O, from what power hast thou this powerful might
150.2: With insufficiency my heart to sway?
150.3: To make me give the lie to my true sight,
150.4: And swear that brightness doth not grace the day?
150.5: Whence hast thou this becoming of things ill,
150.6: That in the very refuse of thy deeds
150.7: There is such strength and warrantise of skill
150.8: That, in my mind, thy worst all best exceeds?
150.9: Who taught thee how to make me love thee more
150.10: The more I hear and see just cause of hate?
150.11: O, though I love what others do abhor,
150.12: With others thou shouldst not abhor my state:
150.13: If thy unworthiness raised love in me,
150.14: More worthy I to be beloved of thee.
151.1: Love is too young to know what conscience is;
151.2: Yet who knows not conscience is born of love?
151.3: Then, gentle cheater, urge not my amiss,
151.4: Lest guilty of my faults thy sweet self prove:
151.5: For, thou betraying me, I do betray
151.6: My nobler part to my gross body’s treason;
151.7: My soul doth tell my body that he may
151.8: Triumph in love; flesh stays no farther reason;
151.9: But, rising at thy name, doth point out thee
151.10: As his triumphant prize. Proud of this pride,
151.11: He is contented thy poor drudge to be,
151.12: To stand in thy affairs, fall by thy side.
151.13: No want of conscience hold it that I call
151.14: Her “love” for whose dear love I rise and fall.
152.1: In loving thee thou know’st I am forsworn,
152.2: But thou art twice forsworn, to me love swearing,
152.3: In act thy bed-vow broke and new faith torn
152.4: In vowing new hate after new love bearing.
152.5: But why of two oaths’ breach do I accuse thee,
152.6: When I break twenty? I am perjured most;
152.7: For all my vows are oaths but to misuse thee
152.8: And all my honest faith in thee is lost,
152.9: For I have sworn deep oaths of thy deep kindness,
152.10: Oaths of thy love, thy truth, thy constancy,
152.11: And, to enlighten thee, gave eyes to blindness,
152.12: Or made them swear against the thing they see;
152.13: For I have sworn thee fair; more perjured I,
152.14: To swear against the truth so foul a lie!
153.1: Cupid laid by his brand, and fell asleep:
153.2: A maid of Dian’s this advantage found,
153.3: And his love-kindling fire did quickly steep
153.4: In a cold valley-fountain of that ground;
153.5: Which borrow’d from this holy fire of Love
153.6: A dateless lively heat, still to endure,
153.7: And grew a seeting bath, which yet men prove
153.8: Against strange maladies a sovereign cure.
153.9: But at my mistress’ eye Love’s brand new-fired,
153.10: The boy for trial needs would touch my breast;
153.11: I, sick withal, the help of bath desired,
153.12: And thither hied, a sad distemper’d guest,
153.13: But found no cure: the bath for my help lies
153.14: Where Cupid got new fire⁠—my mistress’ eyes.
154.1: The little Love-god lying once asleep
154.2: Laid by his side his heart-inflaming brand,
154.3: Whilst many nymphs that vow’d chaste life to keep
154.4: Came tripping by; but in her maiden hand
154.5: The fairest votary took up that fire
154.6: Which many legions of true hearts had warm’d;
154.7: And so the general of hot desire
154.8: Was sleeping by a virgin hand disarm’d.
154.9: This brand she quenched in a cool well by,
154.10: Which from Love’s fire took heat perpetual,
154.11: Growing a bath and healthful remedy
154.12: For men diseased; but I, my mistress’ thrall,
154.13: Came there for cure, and this by that I prove,
154.14: Love’s fire heats water, water cools not love.
